newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Farmers press for Ivorian coffee, cocoa reforms.
newsitem.headline: Farmers press for Ivorian coffee, cocoa reforms.

text.p: Ivory Coast's largest farm union SYNAGCI is meeting ministers and exporters to push for more farmer control over cocoa and coffee prices and marketing, the union's president said on Friday.

"Farmers should be paid at least 50 percent of the average export price," SYNAGCI president Cisse Locine told Reuters. "We don't mind lower prices when world rates are down, but the reverse is never applied."

Farm cooperatives should be vetted before being licensed, paid a premium over existing buyers' commissions by exporters and given tax breaks to encourage farmers' groups to compete directly with exporters, he said.

The Caistab marketing board should set up a port quality arbitration panel to resolve disputes between buyers and sellers, use its surplus funds to finance farmers' pre-season costs and encourage the setting up of an independent agricultural bank, he added.
Farmers representatives are particularly critical of prices paid for coffee in the 1996/97 (Oct-Sept) season.

The Caistab opened the season about six weeks late in mid-November, and set its guide farmgate price more in line with world rates than in 1995/96, when exporters received large price support payments.
The price was cut by 200 CFA a kilo to 495 CFA as world prices tumbled ahead of a new year rally. Output was forecast 50,000 tonnes up on the 180,000 tonnes produced in 1995/96.

Locine said about 85,000 tonnes of coffee had been bought by upcountry buyers and exporters for less than the official 1996/97 (Oct-Sept) guide price. Port arrivals totalled about 175,000 by late March.
"We need an arbitration panel with trained Caistab agents to mediate when large price adjustments are made by exporters," said Locine. "Independent quality checks are not working."
Buyers say prices of 320-400 CFA kilo reflected quality problems resulting from unselective harvesting, the impact of rains on drying operations in late 1996 and poor sorting of beans.
"The guide price was for export-quality beans only," said one exporter, adding that large volumes were returned to farmers in early 1997 for re-sorting and winnowing.
Exporters want the Caistab to introduce a new, separate price structure for low grades of coffee to remove confusion, but Locine said quality concerns had been exaggerated.
"There was bad coffee in some areas because exporters have not supplied farmers with enough sacks since distribution was liberalised, so some was stored badly," he said.

Unions say farm cooperatives still offer farmers a way to compete directly against exporters and retain control over coffee and cocoa marketing -- despite the recent collapse of one of the largest cooperative groups, SOGEPAG.

An export guarantee requirement of 25 CFA per kilo should be cut or shelved for cooperatives, while commissions paid by exporters to upcountry buyers should be raised from around 32 CFA to 50 for cooperatives, he said.
SYNAGCI would ask the government to strengthen training for cooperatives and publish a weekly coffee price bulletin for farmers.
Ivory Coast has commissioned a report on liberalisation of coffee marketing but delivery has been delayed since January.
"If the market was properly liberalised, prices to farmers would automatically rise much closer to world rates," said one industry buyer.
